claims.text: Accelerated coupled degradation is primarily driven by preferential oxidation at phase boundaries.
Interphase regions act as natural galvanic sites.
Oxidation mechanically compromises the interphase regions.
Mechanical weakening of oxidized interfaces exacerbates wear in a positive feedback loop.
The initial alloy has distinct heterogeneous phases separated by sharp interfaces.
Elevated-temperature exposure promotes oxidation and enhanced atomic diffusivity.
Galvanic coupling at phase boundaries localizes oxidation and initiates mechanical weakening.
At elevated temperature, galvanic differences accelerate oxidation along phase boundaries and cause preferential corrosion.
Oxidized interphase regions are more susceptible to wear damage.
Corrosion amplifies wear and wear reciprocally amplifies corrosion.
The conventional multiphase alloy will exhibit greater overall degradation than the homogenized baseline.
The conventional multiphase alloy will exhibit greater wear-related mass loss than the homogenized baseline.
The conventional multiphase alloy will exhibit greater corrosion penetration than the homogenized baseline.
The combined degradation will be synergistic rather than merely additive.
Homogenization can minimize phase-boundary contrast and local galvanic effects while retaining a similar overall composition.
The proposed effect will be most pronounced when high temperature, mechanical wear, and an oxidation-promoting corrosive environment occur together.
The quantitative increase in degradation and the magnitude of synergy may vary with environmental parameters.
A controlled comparison should test conventional multiphase and homogenized specimens under identical combined elevated-temperature wear-corrosion conditions.
Failure of the homogenized alloy to reduce both wear and corrosion significantly would falsify the proposed primary mechanism.
Absence of localized phase-boundary oxidation would falsify the proposed mechanism.
